subsubtopic: PROPOSED WITHHOLDING OF APPROVAL FOR OIL DRILLING IN BEAUFORT SEA PENDING INQUIRY INTO ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to Standing Order 43. The report of Environment Canada dated January 14, 1976, states that offshore drilling in the Beaufort Sea could result in a blowout which would go uncontrolled for a period of at least one year and take up to three years to control, resulting in a massive kill of seals, birds, whales, polar bears and other wildlife, further denuding the capacity of natives to live from the land. In view of the fact that the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs intends to conduct hearings for six communities in three days in the north making the consultation process a farce, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn):
That approval be withheld from any company for offshore drilling until a full parliamentary inquiry has been held into the environmental effects of such drilling and further that the terms of reference of the Berger commission be expanded to include the subject of offshore drilling.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a very important motion and I am convinced that no member will dare reject it.
Considering that mankind proceeds from the same Creator and that we are all united one another and living in the same world, our ethnicity, our language and our religion notwithstanding, and considering also that Canadians are ever sensitive to the calamities striking their fellow citizens and other nationalities, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That this House keep a minute of silence as a mark of sympathy for the victims of the Maritimes and the victims in Guatemala heavily devastated by an earthquake, and that this House also urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs to extend to the hard hit people our deepest sympathy.

subsubtopic: FLOODING OF SKAGIT VALLEY BY SEATTLE LIGHT AND POWER-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the decision by a United States court that the Seattle Light and Power Company be granted permission to raise the Ross Dam by 100 feet, which will entail the flooding of over 5,000 acres of the upper Skagit Valley which, according to the report of the International Joint Commission tabled in this House on December 17, 1971, would have far reaching and permanent effects on the environment of the Skagit Valley, what steps does the government intend to take to prevent the flooding of this important and environmentally vulnerable area of British Columbia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FLOODING OF SKAGIT VALLEY BY SEATTLE LIGHT AND POWER-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of points to be made in reply to the question. The United States Federal Power Commission, operating within the context of United States law, has completed its hearings on Seattle's application for a licence to raise Ross Dam. Just two days ago, the federal commission judge hearing the case handed down his decision approving the application. There is a period of 30 days during which exception could be taken to the ruling and then a period of 30 days within which the commission must act to grant the licence or otherwise. If the Federal Power Commission does grant a

February 6, 1976
Oral Questions
licence the matter can be raised in the United States Courts.
I should point out, also, that an application by the Province of British Columbia to overturn the 1942 order of the International Joint Commission approving the raising of the Ross Dam is being held in abeyance by the IJC pending the outcome of discussions which are taking place between British Columbia and Seattle. To make one more point, when the President and the Prime Minister met in Washington, it was agreed that the best way to deal with this question would be through negotiations between the Province of British Columbia and Seattle. These negotiations are still under way and we shall be having discussions on the federal side with provincial officials on the whole question of the Skagit at a very early date.

subsubtopic: FLOODING OF SKAGIT VALLEY BY SEATTLE LIGHT AND POWER-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT
speechtext: Having regard to the statement which was made by the former Secretary of State for External Affairs, the present President of the Privy Council, on February 13, 1971 that before any dam construction which would cause flooding in the Skagit Valley could begin, approval must first be given by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. I want to ask the minister whether that legal interpretation put forward by his predecessor expresses the view held by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs and, if so, whether he or the Prime Minister can assure the House that no such approval will be given either by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources or by any other department of the Canadian government.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FLOODING OF SKAGIT VALLEY BY SEATTLE LIGHT AND POWER-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT
speechtext: I have no reason to question the opinion expressed by my predecessor although, to be honest, I have not considered that particular point. There are a number of contingencies which would have to be dealt with before we reach the point which the hon. member put forward as calling for a final decision by the government.

speechtext:

The Council of Canadian Filmmakers in a statement on August 23 viewed with alarm the situation in their industry and said in part that the situation had been aggravated by several events. subtopic: VOLUNTARY QUOTA SYSTEM FOR FOREIGN FILMS- POSSIBILITY OF CHANGE IN POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Secretary of State could inform the House whether he is planning any action with Mr. Harold Greenberg or the officials of his department, since the CCFM has said that the officials of the Department of the Secretary of State have repeatedly lied to the CCFM when it has expressed fears that plans were afoot for the kind of voluntary agreement which the minister did announce on August 5. subtopic: VOLUNTARY QUOTA SYSTEM FOR FOREIGN FILMS- POSSIBILITY OF CHANGE IN POLICY
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, but I think the hon. member's question is somewhat out of date. The Canadian Council of Filmmakers is perfectly aware of the fact that this chamber is not in a position to legislate quotas over theatres in this country. They come under the jurisdiction of the provinces. They were trying to lobby the provinces to institute quotas in the ten provinces. That effort was not successful. I felt very strongly that some form of quota was necessary. What I was able to do in the interim was make an arrangement through the Canadian Film Development Corporation for a quota which will be observed, obviously not under the aegis of law but which will be observed, and which will be monitored and the results made public through Famous Players and Odeon. That seems to me to be an improvement over where we were. It may not be exactly as much as the Canadian Council of Filmmakers would want.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my reason for speaking is that I support wholeheartedly the subamendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt), a motion which has the effect of removing the censorship aspect of this legislation. I am sure that by doing this we are now getting down to the philosophical aspect of this bill. This is what is of such great concern to people on this side of the House and several members on the government side.
Another reason for speaking in this debate is that I have received, as have many other hon. members, literally hundreds of letters from constituents. I feel I would be less than responsible if I did not rise to express their views on this very important piece of legislation. Every letter has asked that I, as a member of parliament, do all in my power to block legislation that will have the effect of forcing Time and Reader's Digest, as we know them in their present form, out of Canada. It is true the American editions would continue to be published and would be sold in Canada. That point has been made by the supporters of this bill. But that is not the real point. Madam Speaker. The thing that Canadians are upset about is the fact that the Canadian editions, as we know them, will be removed from the bookstores and the mail of Canada. Canadians want the Canadian edition because of its content.
The issue which should trouble us most is the totalitarian nature of the government's legislation. Over half a million copies of Time are circulated in Canada. This is a very large circulation, by any standard, for a country like ours. These are copies which are printed in this country, though the largest part, by far, of the editorial copy originates in Time news bureaux in the United States and around the world. Canadians like myself have deliberately chosen this publication because it provides a window on the world which no Canadian publication can ever hope to emulate-least of all Maclean's with its effete, simpering kind of Canadianism. We need the Time kind of journalism at least as much, if not more, than the sort of thing Maclean's keeps offering us.
I have read Maclean's for at least half a dozen years and I think I understand its approach to journalism. If some hon. members have read Time magazine's 1975 account of the United States government's fiasco in Viet Nam, in terms of sober and, ultimately, health-giving reporting, I think they will understand what it is about a publication such as this which has made so many of us reach for it rather than for Maclean's.
February 6, 1976

I understand the government's position is that to qualify as a Canadian publication a magazine in this country would need to be 80 per cent different from the parent, United States publication, and 75 per cent Canadian-owned. Applied to Time, this rule would obviously mean that the magazine would cease to be. By introducing such rules the government would so affect-totally remake, so to speak-the magazine that Time could no longer continue in the form in which we have chosen to receive it. This is a form of muzzling of the press which we should view seriously. Already we are exposed to many extremist voices in this country. This legislation would make us more susceptible to them and would not give us easy access to publications with a large world view. This bill is opening the door for the narrowest kind of Canadianism and to the strongly ideological kind of journalism which is becoming increasingly prevalent in this country.
Most frequently overlooked is the fact that Time and Reader's Digest have not been given special advantages. These magazines competed in the Canadian marketplace in the same way as other publications. This issue has been presented to the Canadian public in such a way that many feel genuinely that advertisers in Time and Reader's Digest have had tax advantages which advertisers in Canadian publications did not have. Canadians should know that this is not the case. Time and Reader's Digest are being placed in a position of tremendous competitive disadvantage in the hope, as the government likes to believe, that advertisers will take their advertising from these two publications and place it in fully Canadian-owned publications. Taken by itself, that is a most doubtful assumption. We ought to view such attempted manipulation of the press with the utmost seriousness. The free press ought to be one of our most cherished possessions, jealously defended. In a very real sense, Canadians are being deprived of their freedom of choice.
The government's action reminds one more of a totalitarian regime than a truly open democracy. Such action by a Canadian government gives me a great sense of foreboding. The outcome will very likely be that Time and Reader's Digest-certainly the former-will, for all practical purposes, be legislated out of the country by means of economic levers. Canadians will have been deprived of one part of their freedom of choice. One more step will have been taken along the road to repressive action, and all this will have been done without guaranteeing the very thing the government is ostensibly concerned about, namely, a Canadian magazine industry with strong economic viability.
Why are Canadians so concerned about what is happening? Originally, I suggest, the minister intended to force both publications out of this country. Reader's Digest is the best family magazine that enters Canadian homes. It is a welcome visitor, an old friend. For the time being the magazine has been reprieved. Personally, I condemn the method by which this was done. It is not spelled out in legislation. It is open to any future minister of national revenue to reverse such a decision. How would he decide, after a bad night, say, or a bad day, when this matter could come up for decision again?
Non-Canadian Publications

speechtext:
The ministers concerned ought to consider the views of departmental experts, but they ought also to consider the views of the Canadian people. I suggest that they have paid too much attention to the views of the periodicals' association which has an axe to grind and wants to promote its own interests. I suggest that the desires of the Canadian people should prevail. The government should pay more heed than it has to the wishes of Canadians. I should like to put on record the views of certain people who wrote to me communicating their concern about the matter we are discussing. First, may I read the letter of the Reverend Peter Brouwer, who wrote:
With respect to the government's intention to rescind section 19(2) of the Income Tax Act, I wish to express my strong objection. We appreciate and enjoy Reader's Digest and Time magazine a great deal and I hate to see it go or hurt in any way.
As far as we are concerned, there is nothing comparable that can replace them, especially Reader's Digest. It has a good percentage of Canadian content and we would be deprived of that if RD would have to go.
Reader's Digest, I feel, does our country a very worth-while service. It gives work for many Canadian workers and writers.
If the government really wants to strengthen the Canadian magazine industry, let them come up with something comparable even if it means a little extra help. I have nothing against that-
He says that penalizing good, bona fide foreign magazines which try hard to give good Canadian content, is wrong. He ends the letter by saying:
-And why should we be subjected to such arbitrary government interference?
Please, let both Reader's Digest and Time magazine keep their present status.
Next, let me read a letter from an educator, Sister The-rese Messner of St. Patrick's separate school in Caledonia. She writes:

February 6, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
As an educator, I am an avid reader of the Reader's Digest and use it frequently in my English classes, so therefore I would hate to see this publication discontinued in Canada.
She asks, would I please, when section 19(2) of the Income Tax Act disallowing, as a business expense, advertising placed by Canadian companies in the Digest is debated, keep this in mind. This magazine helps our children, she says. The third letter concerning Time and Reader's Digest is from a lawyer. He writes:
Dear Bill:
I spoke to you last Friday to voice my views about the attitude that the government is taking toward Time and Reader's Digest. I am not a constant reader of the latter although I have been a subscriber to Time since I was at law school in the late 1930s.
I pointed out to you that one of the commendable things that Time did during the war was to establish what they called-if my memory serves me correctly-a pony edition. This was an edition printed on fine paper, and carrying no advertising, which they airmailed to their subscribers in the armed forces who were overseas, including the Canadian forces, so that we used to have our edition of Time usually within a week of it hitting the streets in North America.
If the proposed legislation does anything to prohibit Time from carrying on in Canada as they have in the past, I will be most unhappy.
There are many other letters, but I feel these three are a fair example. They are all from responsible citizens. Other Canadians accomplished in journalism, authors, writers, and so on, have expressed the view along the line I have attempted to present today. Editorials in the daily press all across Canada have condemned the principle behind Bill C-58. They say that the 80 per cent difference in content requirement is a form of censorship; it is most dangerous. I would call it a censorship by mathematics. Mathematics is a precise science dealing in figures. Here we are talking about ideas and literary content. How could a magazine be censored by mathematics? In my opinion, the officials of Revenue Canada are the least qualified to do this of any government department.
As I said a few moments ago, one of the most qualified people in this House to do this would be the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. She has many years of experience, and a good reputation as a journalist. We should listen to what she is saying. Why does the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) not consult her before putting a mathematical value on content? The hon. member to whom I referred was not even permitted to be a member of the committee and to make a contribution to it. The government whip is usually a congenial person even though he has a rather loud voice. I hope she was not intimidated by his voice. Surely the whip should have seen the reason and should have permitted her views to be expressed.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Advertising costs should be deductible. The competitors of Time and Reader's Digest claim that those magazines have an unfair advantage in attracting advertisers. That is not so. The reason for advertising in those magazines does not have anything to do with the cost. The fact is that the cost of such ads are deductible, in the same way that advertisers can deduct for advertising in Canadian magazines. The advantage of deductibility is the same for all. The compelling reason lies 
in the fact that these two magazines have the greatest circulation and readership; therefore, there is the greatest possible exposure for advertisers.
I wish to refer to the comments of the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay (Mr. Johnston) whom Your Honour censured the other day, if I may be so bold as to say that. He did not have the opportunity to make his point. He stated that article after article in Saturday Night expressed the Canadian scene in a way that simply turned off readers. Having read one or two issues of that magazine, I found it a most destructive and demoralizing view of the Canadian scene. Maclean's is often in the same category. Nobody wants to be continually fed this sort of thing. The writers in Canadian magazines are what I call iconoclasts: they want to tear down anything that detracts; they do not give Canadians a sense of well-being or a sense of being proud to be Canadian. It is for this reason that Time and Reader's Digest attract the readership they do. This is why advertisers use them to reach the Canadian people.
Magazines such as Maclean's need only to improve their format. I would be less than honest if I did not admit that they made some effort in this regard, although they still turn me off. They must improve their format in order to appeal to a larger cross-section of the Canadian people. If they do that, they will certainly increase their circulation and readership. They will then attract advertisers and get their share of the advertising dollar.

I have shown that Bill C-58 flies in the face of what grassroots Canadians really want. It is important to have another look at the "content" interpretation based on the 80 per cent content rule, or to simply remove it altogether as this subamendment suggests. That is why I support it. There needs to be much greater precision in defining what the government is talking about. It cannot be left to the whim of any minister. Surely it is not beyond the competence of the departmental officials to devise a precise way of indicating what they want accomplished. It would be far better to remove this provision altogether.
I admit that the present minister has good intentions. Previous speakers have complimented him. I know him as an honourable minister who wants to do what is right. I feel he had a gun held to his head, perhaps by the Secretary of State or the cabinet, and this compelled him to take this avenue of accomplishing the removal of Time and Reader's Digest from the Canadian scene.
There is the threat of closure. To what end? Reader's Digest will live, thanks to the minister and the special arrangement he has made. Let me say, however, that we want to know about it in more precise terms. The Canadian edition of Time will perhaps disappear. Canadians will have lost a publication which gives us a view of the world. As I said before, it is a window on the world. The advertis-

ing revenue accruing to other Canadian magazines such as Maclean's will remain essentially the same, for the reasons I have given. I will support all amendments and subamendments which have the effect of permitting Time and Reader's Digest to continue to provide intelligent, interesting reading to thinking Canadians.

Madam Speaker, in rising to speak in support of motion No. 4, placed before the House by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) and seconded by myself, I think it becomes quite obvious that I have serious misgivings about certain aspects of the bill that is before us. This is a somewhat difficult and delicate role for a backbencher to play. For this reason, and at the outset of my remarks, I want to express my support and encouragement of the two ministers involved who have been faced with the unenviable task of attempting to grapple with yet another aspect of our developing Canadian nationhood-that relating to the status of the publishing industry in this country and the promotion and sustenance of greater Canadian talent in that area.
There is one other general comment I would like to make at this point, and I feel this very sincerely. I feel it is an indication of the real strength of the government, and of the party which forms the government-of which I am proud to be a part-that, as a backbencher of rather lowly rank, I can rise in this chamber and speak freely and express my concern about specific aspects of this legislation, even when such concern extends to the point where the member may find it beyond the bounds of his considered judgment to be able to support the legislation in the final stages of debate.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
I want to talk on several aspects of the bill, but first I would like to speak about the intent of the legislation as I understand it. My understanding is that it is intended to assist Canadian newspapers and the periodical industry, to promote Canadian talent and to take a further step in our development as an independent and interdependent nation. So what did we do? Ten years ago we introduced a 75 per cent ownership clause. This was the key. This was the clause which exempted, at the time, two prominent international magazines then on the market in Time and Reader's Digest. It was a move in the right direction. It was a move which had the general support of Canadians.
What are we doing now? We are taking this one step further: we are introducing Bill C-58 and we are saying that the exemption given ten years ago to those particular periodicals is not valid today and that it should be withdrawn. Basically, that is all that the legislation says. The legislation as it is proposed at the present time really changes no other aspect. So Bill C-58 is really intended to complete the job which was started ten years ago.
The problem arises with the introduction of a new definition which really came before us some ten months after the bill was introduced. It is not a factor in the bill itself, but it is clear-and I think the minister deserves credit for having made this clear-that it is going to be part of the regulations that will be followed as the bill is adminis-
Non-Canadian Publications
tered. The key phrase in this connection is "not substantially the same". For the last ten years there has never been a test, as I understand it, of that particular phraseology in the Income Tax Act. It was never queried. This was probably one reason why the legislation worked so well. It was never queried until this spring, and at the time it was queried my understanding is that departmental officials in the Department of National Revenue, in their usual able way, looked at it and said, "Well, we would interpret this as being 50 per cent different."
That was a reasonable conclusion, arrived at by reasonable people. The senior officials in the Department of National Revenue are, indeed, very reasonable people. My understanding is that, based on that ruling, one of those international magazines, namely, Time, proceeded to arrange its affairs so that it could live with Bill C-58. In other words, it was prepared to become a Canadian magazine 75 per cent owned and controlled in Canada and it was prepared to change its format dramatically so as to have a 50 per cent Canadian content. In the case of Reader's Digest, I understand they never did give that indication; they never did indicate, until very recently, that they had any intention of Canadianizing their operation as Time had done. Then, late in October, the government came up with this 80 per cent factor, and this, I suggest, drastically changed the rules of the game.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
I am not a lawyer, but it is not at all clear to me how something that is "not substantially the same" has to be "80 per cent different." It seems to me that if the legislators in 1965-and I was not among them-had wanted "not substantially the same" to mean something other than a normal person would deem it to mean, they would have inserted such definition into the legislation at the time. Surely, if they had thought in terms of 80 per cent different or 75 per cent different, or whatever, they would have indicated as much and put it into the bill at that time. However, they did not, and I think that is an important point.
My objection is that we should be forced to accept as an understanding, as we review and pass Bill C-58, that even though there is no change in the bill itself, based on the 1965 "not substantially the same" terminology, that part of what we are doing must be deemed to change that situation. In other words, we understand there is to be an accompanying regulation which will say that from now on "not substantially the same", regardless of what it meant in the past, will from now on mean "80 per cent different."
The nub of the issue, in my view, is that this is really not what parliament wants at all, and I do not think it is really what the Canadian people want. That is why I am supporting the "60 per cent different" terminology in motion No. 4. I believe it refers to 40 per cent the other way, but effectively 60 per cent is the content factor included in motion No. 4. If the government proposes to get into the content game, that seems to be a much more rational and acceptable approach and one which contains a reasonable degree of fairness and equity. I believe we need to put this into legislation if we are going to do it at all.
Madam Speaker, there are a number of points I wish to cover. My time is limited, so I propose to discuss now some

February 6, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
aspects of the content provisions of the legislation which are of particular concern to me. Following that, I shall probably come back to another matter relating to the "international pool" development which is now applicable to Reader's Digest. But I will skip that for the moment. Let me speak of the content rule. I want to talk for a few moments about the matter of freedom of the press. I know that the last thing in the minister's mind is that any enactment of parliament under his direction would in any way attempt to limit the freedom of the press as we understand it in Canada. Yet I submit that, wilfully or not, imposing this 80 per cent content factor really does have an effect in that direction. It must be accepted that in future, assuming the passage of Bill C-58 in its present form, Canadians engaged in publishing periodicals or newspapers in this country will not be free to publish what they wish and to stay in business, simply because advertising revenues will not be available to them unless they conform to a specific government requirement imposed by parliament.
Normally, my concern about this issue would not be so great as it is had I not had a recent international experience during which I talked first-hand to the people who knew whereof they spoke. I refer to complete withdrawal of the freedom of the press under a parliamentary system not very different from our own. This experience remains with me and will never, likely, be erased. I was also amazed to read recently of the freedom threats that were implied by a reputable Canadian editor to have been directed to the press around the free world in 1974. He referred to such countries as Portugal, Greece, Lebanon, Iraq, Turkey, Thailand, Cambodia, South Viet Nam and Africa, among others. Madam Speaker, without further elaboration of this point, which I know will be disagreeable to many members of this House, I just want to say I agree with the concept that magazine readership must be earned and that it cannot be legislated by government.
The next point I would like to touch on is one relating to advertising dollars. Until quite recently I was under the impression that these two international magazines which have been of such concern to us were drawing a very large proportion of advertising dollars in the consumer magazine advertising business in Canada. I now understand, from what I consider to be a reliable source, that the total obtained by these two magazines in 1975 was 20 per cent, compared with the combination of the Toronto Star and the Maclean's group which drew 47 per cent.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext: Of what?

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Advertising revenue. Time, the magazine that now seems to be the only one under the gun, drew 12 per cent on its own. The point is that Canadian magazines are indeed growing quite well and it may really be doubtful whether the content protection is basically needed for them. From a circulation point of view, however, it is clear that Canadian magazines would be happy to see the disappearance of those that have an international base, something that in my view will not actually occur because I do not think that the readership of Time-Reader's Digest being no longer affected-will drop by a single subscription.

I should like to make a few remarks about what I consider to be the counterproductive nature of this legislation, and I am particularly referring to the 80 per cent factor. Presumably, the intent of the 80 per cent is to keep any new international periodicals out of the country, or at least to prevent them establishing a Canadian-owned and operated organization. It was also the intent that Reader's Digest would probably have to fold its Canadian operation, though this matter has now been resolved.
My view, as I mentioned earlier, is that the readership of Time magazine will not decrease by one subscription. So really what we have done is to eliminate not only the possibility but, indeed, the firm and stated intent of a major international newsmagazine to Canadianize its operations and vastly change the format of its publication so as inevitably to enhance development of the Canadian periodical industry, with all its offshoots in the area of Canadian talent and business to Canadian enterprises that that would bring. Surely we are not looking at this time for a means to lessen economic activity in this country. By throwing out the existing Canadian edition we are even going so far as to take away whatever economic benefit may have existed in the country. At the same time we are effectively saying no to the potential of a much more Canadianized operation in all respects. I simply do not understand the thinking that has led to this kind of development, Madam Speaker. To me, it makes no economic sense whatsoever, particularly at this point in time.
I would now like to speak about the creation of a precedent that I see arising from the 80 per cent question. As a chartered accountant engaged in a number of industry settings prior to my election to this House in July, 1974, I had a good deal of interaction with the Income Tax Act and with the officers at all levels of Revenue Canada who have had the responsibility over the years of administering this very complex statute, which has become even more complex since 1972. I have developed a great respect and esteem for the senior officers of Revenue Canada. In fact, it is, I think, the real strength of our taxation system that we have been able to entice and hold people of such calibre to manage and administer the legislation that brings in the revenues of this country.
I believe it was the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Abbott) who drew the attention of the House to the fact that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) and his officers are frequently making interpretations under the Income Tax Act. They do this under the regulations that accompany the act. This is part and parcel of the difficult role which they are frequently called upon to play. However, Madam Speaker, in my view-and this has been my experience over the years-the government has normally attempted to restrict these regulations to accompanying sections of the Income Tax Act where in fact it was not possible to cover in the actual law the varying sorts of problems that might arise in practice. Yet that, surely, is not the case here.
It follows that the argument relating to the frequency of use of ministerial discretion under the normal operations of the Income Tax Act does not apply in this case. Here, is simply a question as to whether the figure of 80 per cent, 60 per cent, 50 per cent, 40 per cent or whatever should be inserted into the legislation. To not insert a definite figure,
February 6, 1976

in my view, is attempting to do by ministerial discretion what we are not prepared to do in the normal parliamentary process. This grates me, Madam Speaker, and I believe it is a most undesirable precedent for this House to adopt.
I should like to say a few words about the timing of this legislation. I do not find it difficult to support that portion of the motion put forward by the hon. member for Ontario which simply would give a reasonable amount of time to both Time and Reader's Digest to enable them to arrange their ownership affairs in order to meet the requirements of a proposed piece of legislation that will conceivably be passed into law within the next few months.
To suggest, as I believe has been suggested, that an effective date of January 1, 1976, would be fair under the circumstances, in view of the fact that these periodicals have been aware for some time of the intentions of the government in regard to this bill, is in my view stretching the credibility of such an argument far beyond any bounds that can be construed as in any way being fair and reasonable. It is my sincere hope that businesses operating in Canada will always be in a position where they can depend on the laws of the country, as they may exist from time to time, in carrying out their operations and making business decisions that may indeed be fundamental to the continuation of such operations in the country, as is indeed the case with Bill C-58.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I should like to make a few points quite clear in regard to my position on this bill. First, I consider it not only a privilege but a responsibility to speak out in this important forum when confronted by an item of legislation that, in my best judgment, is not in the interests of the public at large. Second, I want again to express my confidence and my satisfaction as a member on the government side in the completely open and almost supportive stand that this government is prepared to take in regard to members who from time to time disagree with specific items of legislation.
My last point is that I want to make it aboundantly clear that I have absolutely no axe to grind with, or on behalf of, any existing periodicals operating in this country which will be seriously affected by this legislation, or indeed with any other publications of international repute which will now be precluded from establishing a Canadian-owned and operated enterprise in the future. My only interest is to see that any legislation in which I participate as a member of parliament during my time on the Hill is truly in the public interest. I do not believe that the existing format of Bill C-58 is so, with specific reference to some of the trappings associated with the bill. I urge members of the House to support motion No. 4 which has been put forward by the hon. member for Ontario.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, probably no piece of legislation has generated a more strenuous and informative debate than the debate which has evolved around this particular piece of legislation, its amendments and the motions associated with it. Perhaps at no time in parliamentary history, both through the expressions of members of the House and expressions supported by communications, be they verbal or written, has there ever been such a preponderance of evidence that the government is taking a course that is not approved by the people and which is not necessarily in their best interests.
Non-Canadian Publications
I think it would be rare indeed if one were to look through the records of this House and find that speech after speech from the side of the proponents of a piece of legislation have criticized and complained about the effects it would have upon them, their constituents and Canada at large.
This bill has been criticized authentically and in documentary fashion in respect of its difficulties of administration, the broadness of possible interpretation and the precarious position in which those that survive may find themselves after this legislation has been brought to bear. It does not necessarily apply only to foreign-owned structures, but it could conceivably apply to Canadian structures within the printing industry. It could, for instance, in many daily newspapers find people from the Department of National Revenue carefully looking over the paper to see how much has been generated by local reporters, how much has been generated on the editorial page by editorials copied from abroad, how much has come from UPI and other foreign sources, and how much has been picked up and merely rewritten to create an interest for the reader of that particular publication.
It is very broad in the impact that it might have while it is officially levelled at two publications in this country. It leads me to wonder whether it is in the interest of Canada, in the interest of the Liberal party or in the interest of some academics, regardless of the interest of the rest of Canada, that this particular bill is now before us. Has it got something to do with the philosophy of the publisher, or has it got something to do with the philosophy of the writers?
I think the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay (Mr. Johnston) made some very pertinent remarks in respect of the interesting aspects of articles which were published in Saturday Night. I think he defined quite adequately why that magazine has not had economic success. He explained why a multitude of Canadians would not read it in large enough numbers to attract advertising, regardless of the competition that existed.
So is it philosophy? Is it because a Sunday school teacher may on occasion take an article from the Reader's Digest to his class? Is it because a minister could quote that magazine effectively as he speaks from the pulpit? Is it because in the main Reader's Digest has been a supporter of the free enterprise system? Is it because on occasion it has attacked a political philosophy that we do not share in this country? Is that the reason? There is no other obvious reason, because you cannot legislate an effective press, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) only moments ago: you just cannot legislate an effective press or an effective magazine industry.
Let us take again the case of Time. Time magazine also has been a free enterprise structure. It has abhorred the interference of government in the lives of the people. It has, I must say, been a very vicious attacker of a former leader of our party and, in effect, in its attack has supported the present government and aided and abetted its election. It is now getting its throat cut.
Is that because it is philosophically not in line with the government of today? We cannot help but wonder about

these things. Is this another way of removing an obstacle from the minds of Canadians, an obstacle which might be in the way of the re-election of this government, because philosophically the mood of this government certainly is not reflected by articles which one reads in either of the magazines concerned? Certainly neither of these magazines would support this in a free editorial structure, and they are not free at this moment in time. They would scarcely dare open their mouths except in a plea for their support. Certainly they are not free at this moment in time to editorialize without being further considered guilty by a government of this structure and this nature.
There are in Canada a multitude of magazines which serve Canadians on a regional or relatively local basis. Among these magazines one would have to consider the Atlantic Advocate. It has been an authentic magazine with an attractive readership. It is a magazine which is,taken to school, to the historical society and to other organizations as an example of authentic literature in respect of the area which it serves. It has given historic and current articles to the readership of that area which are of great significance. It has, without fear or favour requested, presented articles which attack the government of the day and which support the government of the day. It has represented the broad view of the editorial staff of this structure which has made it an attractive magazine read by maritimers whether at home or abroad.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that if the national structure of the magazine industry in Canada were to follow the same pattern, Canadians would be seeking these magazines out and they would not be seeking those of foreign ownership or those of foreign publication. It is from this point of view, I think, that this House must consider what is good or what is bad for Canadians, because we cannot legislate change in the philosophies of those who write the present magazines.
I should like to take an example, as did the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay, of an article in Maclean's magazine by Mr. Harry Bruce, who I agree has done some good writing in Canada. He wrote an article about the rural community in which I live. That article discussed the principal economic support of that community and of tens of thousands of people around us, including an important part of the constituency of Victoria-Madawaska. The hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles) described this article extremely well when be wondered whether these were iconoclasts or whether they were looking for the things they could criticize and not looking for the good side.
This article pertained to the McCain food industry. Let me say at this moment that I have no conflict of interest because of any pecuniary interest in that corporation- none whatsoever. I happen to be one of the distant cousins to which they have never extended the use of their chequebook and are not likely to. I am certainly not taking their part; I am taking the part of the economic stability of the community in which I live. The national image which was created by the article written by Harry Bruce was detrimental not only to the company concerned but to the whole area because he criticized, while looking for nothing 
good, and he discovered virtually all the bad one could find. May I call it one o'clock?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the noon-hour I was mentioning an article which referred to one aspect of my constituency in which the subject matter was extremely critical. I submit it was not an in-depth consideration of the subject matter nor a fair consideration of it. The picture presented could reduce the business of the company concerned if the article were to be believed by all its readers. This is an article detrimental to the area in which I live. It is an article to which the owners, publishers, editors and whoever may be responsible did not give proper analysis prior to distribution. This is the kind of article which will not have the magazine read, no matter where published or by whom, and no matter how Canadian it may be. Altogether, too many of these articles appear.
I abhor the basic philosophy of so many people who seek out the bad in an individual, regardless of how good his record may be. I abhor the approach, that seems to be totally negative, where we cannot assess the positive and present that as well. I suppose the classic example in today's American publications would be the assault on the Kennedy's. The Kennedy's may be criticized for their accomplishments in the field for which they are noted, but it is also high time that they were assessed in their daily work rather than in the way they live. If this is a matter of interest to some, and I agree it is, it certainly is not an item of interest to an adequate readership in the Canadian magazine structure which we are talking about, or any other comparable structure anywhere in this world. Those who go for filth will read it, but those who go for information in their reading and expect information from national publications, of course, will not read it and will not be patronized, therefore, by the advertisers who must have readership if they are to obtain value for the money spent.
It has been stated in this House that there is a parallel. I will be repetitive in this regard, inasmuch as I made comparable remarks during an earlier phase of this debate. It has been stated that the materials which flow into the two magazines in this area do so at lower than the total cost. I submit that every magazine in Canada has a purpose to use syndicated columnists, and that every writer in Canada has a purpose to join a syndicated organization whereby his work can be distributed. I submit that if there is theft of our literature from Canada, we should not legislate other literature out but should negotiate a fair deal for Canadian writers and foreign writers, particularly from the United States. This has been mentioned in this debate.
This amendment does not at all correct the structure about which we are objecting. The amendment and the bill refer to an indefinable and only interpretable difference. I submit to you, Madam Speaker, that probably most members of this House could take a pen and, without research,
February 6, 1976

reproduce an article for Reader's Digest or Time magazine that would really accomplish little in result and would convey the full intent of the original author. That would contribute very little to society and would, in return, produce a lower fee for the writer while it would accomplish, in a poorer way, the same purpose. The writer would have condensed it, recondensed it and altered it-and who does not? It is just a matter of basic homework, and the cost of that homework, having been done abroad while some magazine hires a flunkey to do it over again, probably in poorer form. What are we really accomplishing?
I should like to issue a little warning to the minister. While he may be totally and completely dedicated to this cause, a group of his predecessors in cabinet have been equally dedicated to causes only to find, when their government was criticized for that cause, that they no longer held office. Just to cite a few, a gentleman by the name of Benson went across Canada with a white paper with the full backing of the Prime Minister. He was dedicated. He said, "This shall be our law, and this is our white paper." Mr. Benson did not even run for parliament after that. There was a minister of consumer and corporate affairs named Gray, and another fellow by the name of Haidasz. More recently, there was a fellow by the name of Turner. And what about another fellow by the name of Stanbury? I assure the minister that if, perchance, this government happens to experience political repercussions because of the dedication of the minister to a cause opposed by many Canadians, the name which is written at the end of that list may very well be his.
I regret very much that a good friend of mine by the name of Alden Nowland, who is nationally noted as an author, came under some criticism in the course of this debate, but if one is going to write, or if one is going to be in the field of politics, one has to be able to take criticisms and I am sure he will not mind. He has, by long personal sacrifice and dedication to his profession, achieved prominence in Canada, which is a great credit to him. While I reserve the right not to agree with him-and he has, in print, already reserved the right not to agree with me- that in no way interferes with our long-standing personal friendship, and I hope that will remain a mutual situation. However, the criticism merely indicates that the Canadian public has the right to criticize what it reads, and to read it or leave it. Let us read it or leave it, and not legislate any control over it to ram down the throats of Canadians.
This bill has a multitude of weaknesses, including its total unpopularity with many Canadian people-but it is an administrative carte blanche. I do not believe that in any instance we should give to any minister or pair of ministers the right to judge and to put themselves into the position of being both judge and executioner. This is not right. Putting all other criticisms of this legislation aside, the delegation of authority to the minister and the cabinet is, to me, an obnoxious factor in this bill because it is purely and simply a matter of judgment. It is not defined for either the Minister of Finance or the Secretary of State just what might be done with this legislation at any given time in the future. Those who might at some future time come under the influence of this legislation should bear in mind that they are at the whim, pleasure and total person-
Non-Canadian Publications
al disposal of those who make personal judgments in the execution of their jobs as part of the government structure. It may be the minister or an understrapper of some kind, but this is not legislation which defines the position of any publication in Canada, Time and Reader's Digest included, despite any smoke-filled, backroom deal which may have been made.
It seems to me that there should be international representation on a worldwide basis employed by Canadian publications. If we are to pass this legislation, Canada is entitled to first-hand technical knowledge of Canadians located outside Canada. There is no indication whatsoever that any publication in Canada has the capacity to do this, and if there is the capacity to give us worldwide information perhaps it will have to be in co-operation with other publications from other lands to exchange items of interest in a way which people can find credible. I submit that until such time as a syndicated structure can be established for regional publications, and until such time as our national publications can find the opportunity, the way to co-operate with other national groups either inside or outside Canada to maintain a group of authors who will give Canada credible articles on the world at large, this legislation is totally premature.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) has a distinguished record of supporting the objectives of ensuring that kind of protection for the Canadian periodicals system. Where the hon. member for Ontario might disagree is with the effectiveness of the legislation to reach those objectives. The first question the hon. member raises is why such legislation or regulations are necessary to achieve the objectives. It springs from the context of economic activity on this continent which supports the periodicals industry.
The House recognized this in 1965 when it brought in legislation to correct what otherwise would have been a difficult or impossible situation. If you are producing magazine material for a market of 200 million or 220 million people in North America, as is the case for most publications within the United States, then the cost per article is relatively low because you can write off the cost more widely than what it would be for purchasing the same kind of material of the same standard for a market in Canada of 22 million people. It is a very simple argument.

The cost of material of the same quality on a pro rata basis in the United States is much lower than it could possibly be for publications which operate in Canada.
In that sense, it is very easy to place in Canada foreign material at very low cost to the magazine that wants to use it in Canada, because the cost of producing that material has already been met in a much larger market. In effect, the material could be easily dumped, if there were no regulations or legislation to oppose it, from the United States market into the Canadian market. Revenue to the originator for that material would be gravy, not necessary to cover the cost of the material in the first place.
It is for that reason in 1965 we had a situation of unfair competition. Magazines coming into Canada at a lower cost base could compete effectively against Canadian magazines. The life of the Canadian magazine industry was threatened with this kind of competition. It was going to be impossible for them to survive. One of the witnesses who appeared before the committee in reference to this subject put it very well. He said if you were manufacturing automobiles and had to do that lock, stock and barrel, and there was a competitor down the street who was importing engines which he did not have to pay for, obviously he would be in a superior competitive position. You would not stay in business very long if you had to cover the whole cost of production while the competitor covered only half or a portion of it. The example is quite a good parallel with the magazine industry.
It was for these reasons that changes were made in 1965 to try to ensure that Canadian periodicals had a chance of surviving. That change said to Canadian advertisers, "If you wish to deduct the cost of advertising, it must take place in magazines whose material originates in Canada". There were two major exceptions, Time and Reader's Digest, who were able to have the advantage both of low costs-because they were producing for the North American market-and an advantage in competing against American competitors such as Newsweek because they promised their advertisers a tax deduction which Newsweek and other foreign magazines could not offer.
What we are doing in this legislation is removing that anomaly. It is not a question of censorship, but simply saying "Compete on the same terms as other Canadian magazines or the same terms as non-Canadian magazines. Don't expect the advantages of both. Choose the same footing either of one or the other." It removes the special and advantageous position which those magazines have had.
The hon. member for Ontario says that in practice what we are doing is insisting that 80 per cent of the material originate in Canada, so why not make it 60 per cent? In other words, it is not a question of principle. He is arguing it is all right to be 60 per cent pregnant, but 80 per cent pregnant is not all right. He says he believes 60 per cent would be sufficient to encourage the Canadian periodicals industry. The hon. member for Scarborough West made the same argument. He looked at the percentage of total advertising revenues paid to Time and Reader's Digest and said it was small. It would have been more accurate if he had brought to the House the figures for the periodicals industry. He would have seen that the amount Time and Reader's Digest siphoned off was very significant.
February 6, 1976

If we accepted the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Ontario, I suggest we would create not only a situation in which Time and Reader's Digest would be able to bring in 40 per cent of material originating outside the country, but that virtually every Canadian periodical would ultimately be required to depend more and more heavily on material generated outside this country. That is the major difficulty with the proposal. This difficulty has not been dealt with by hon. members opposite, as far as I can recall, nor has it been greatly stressed by members on this side.
What the amendment would do is set a context which would assure that in order to be able to compete effectively in cost terms, almost every Canadian periodical would have to face a split-run type of situation. If your competitors are able to bring in 40 per cent of their material at high quality and low cost, no Canadian periodical is going to be encouraged to do any better than that, because in doing better than that he will put himself in a difficult cost position in comparison to his competitor.
The suggestion which the hon. member for Ontario is making would not only not assist the production of more Canadian material in the Canadian periodicals industry but it would in fact have the reverse effect. It would lead to less and less Canadian material being produced because it would be cheaper to import it from sources outside the country.
Some members may suggest there is nothing to worry about in that; that we should open the market and let whoever can compete, compete with whatever advantages he has. Some members say that we should let all compete on whatever basis they like in the periodicals industry, communications and in allied areas. I point out that we have decided in other fields that such a course of action would be strongly inimical to the interests of this country.
No doubt it would be cheaper to do away with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the Canadian television system and let ABC, NBC and CBS instal stations in every Canadian city. That would cost less. The stations would still carry local news after the national news, no doubt-the American national news. But we have said that we do not feel this approach would be appropriate. The reason is that we wish to assure, in Canada, access to Canadian material for those who wish to see it. For that reason, we support our broadcasting system and impose content requirements on that broadcasting system in order to ensure that those who wish to see or hear Canadian news, who wish to see the world with the Canadian viewpoint, will be able to do so.
Those listening to this debate might be pardoned for concluding that if this legislation is allowed to pass, Canadians will be unable to receive material describing what is happening outside the country. I suggest that access to U.S. publications is not threatened in our country, what is threatened is the Canadian ability to receive Canadian material and a view of the world through Canadian eyes. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, it would be better to proceed with the argument. Of course the committee worked under restraints. It worked under a time restraint to which all parties agreed. The discussions necessarily took place within that framework. The hon. member loves to feel persecuted. I would simply say there is no reason to impute motives of persecution when all that has happened is that there has been a disagreement of view. The member for Vancouver-Kingsway may march to a different drummer; she should not expect her colleagues to fall all over themselves to dance to her particular tune. I want to pass on briefly to the argument that somehow in the past few days there has been an extraordinary collapse and change of view on the government's part in relation to Reader's Digest. It was quite clear, I believe, to most of us who sat on the committee that if Reader's Digest were prepared to meet the ownership requirements, it could very easily meet the 80 per cent content requirement rule. In fact, it was established before the committee that so long as an article appeared first in the Canadian Reader's Digest, even if it subsequently or almost immediately were to appear in the international edition, it would be classified as material meeting the 80 per cent requirement. This is because the purpose of the requirement was to encourage the generation of material within Canada, and that, in effect, is what is happening under the clarification-not, I would argue, a great change, but a clarification-which was described by the Minister of National Revenue.
There has been no collapse, no great change in government policy. What happened was that Reader's Digest agreed to meet the requirements, which came as no surprise to many of those who sat on the committee. The interpretation provided by the Minister of National Revenue is this: if there is an article in the possession of the Reader's Digest pool, then provided that the rewriting and condensation of it is done by Canadians in Canada, that will be considered as part of the 80 per cent content. This, I would think, was generally clear from the beginning; material which was rewritten, condensed or originated for the Canadian edition would be classified under the 80 per cent substantially different rule.
The criticism that the clarification of the ruling in relation to Reader's Digest indicates the arbitrariness of the legislation and the regulations seems to me to be completely fallacious. If the minister had come to the House and said only that he was presenting legislation which required 
that a periodical be substantially not the same if it was to qualify for that tax advantage, members opposite would have said, "What is 'substantially not the same"1? Why do you not tell us exactly what you mean? What is this pig in the poke you are asking us to buy?" In response to that kind of questioning from the magazines affected and from members of the opposition, the government has indicated what, in its view, the phrase "substantially not the same" means. That is all that has been done. So as not to fudge the issue, so as to be frank with members of the House, the government has said what, in its view, those words mean.
Of course, the opportunity to deal with the courts still exists. Hon. members ask; "What if the court disagrees with your interpretation? Does that mean you abandon the policy? Do you abandon the techniques? Do you abandon the objective?" The government has simply said, "No. Under those circumstances we shall come back with proposed legislation for what we believe is required and what we say now to the House is required." There is no arbitrariness in that position. There is no possibility of changing "substantially not the same" without coming back to the House and seeking approval. The government has been asked to say clearly what the requirements are and what they mean in practical terms. It would have been denying its responsibility if it had simply said, "Those are the words we intend to use. We do not know how they will be interpreted. We have no view as to what their effect will be."

What I want to know, and the hon. member may be able to tell me, is this: as the matter now stands, assuming the bill passes in its present form without any of the amendments being accepted, will that decision be made by a civil servant in the office of the Minister of National Revenue, or will the government pass regulations under the regulatory granting powers in section 221 to prescribe specifically what is the meaning of the words "substantially the same as the contents of an issue of the periodical"? I welcome the question asked by the learned gentleman who is, as we know, a distinguished lawyer. Fortunately, I am not. Some consideration was given to this question in the committee. I hope I shall not mislead the hon. member when I say that the decision, in the first instance, is one taken by tax officials though ultimately determination will be made by members of the government. Perhaps that is what will happen in this case. Considerable material was presented to the committee in an effort to clarify the legal situation. There was a dispute
February 6, 1976

about it. But there was certainly a great deal of material indicating that 75 per cent or 80 per cent would probably be, or could be, on the basis of various cases, particularly in the United States, the criterion for deciding that kind of question. No doubt it was a disputed issue, but there was legal precedent for that kind of criterion.
My point is this. While it would be possible, under the "substantially not the same" clause, for varying interpretations to be made, there is a provision for appeal to the courts respecting that interpretation. Cases will ultimately be decided by the courts; the courts will ultimately determine what that means. What seems to arouse hon. gentlemen opposite is that we have gone further and said that if the courts decide that the 80 per cent is not what "substantially the same" means, then the government would go back to the Commons and ask for the approval of the House of criteria which they believe are necessary to deal with the situation. I do not call that arbitrary or irresponsible. We are saying that the courts and parliament will ultimately decide what is to be done in connection with this matter. As I say, there is nothing arbitrary about it. Ministers reach their decisions within the context of this phrase, whose meaning, ultimately, it is up to the courts to determine. Then Parliament will be asked to change the law. That is hardly shocking. It is for this reason, I suggest, that arguments about arbitrariness and arguments about censorship are not germane to the issue before us. The issue before us is the practicality of the legislation for achieving an objective which most of us in this House share-the encouragement, through advertising revenues, of the Canadian periodical industry.
There are those who disagree that the legislation will have that effect. I would refer them most earnestly to the long and diligent committee consideration which took place on the matter. I believe that if they do this fairly they will find convincing evidence that there will be a significant impact on advertising revenues as a result of this bill, and that changes will be brought about favourable to the industry in Canada. I beg hon. members not to be distracted by false accusations of arbitrariness and censorship which are not germane to the issue. I urge hon. members to give as speedy a passage to the legislation as possible.

The minister has raised a point that is directly at issue and concerns those who serve on the statutory instruments committee. Because of some arbitrary and capricious decisions that were arrived at by the Privy Council Office and other ministers, an artificial definition has been placed on the regulations which places many of them outside our scope. The minister has put his finger right on it.
I would suggest that section 221 does provide that there may be the opportunity, by regulation, to carry out the purposes of the act. I think that has been interpreted in the past in a wide enough way to permit the government, if it sees fit, in accordance with section 221 (j), to deal with this issue and lay down regulations as to what in its opinion constitutes a publication or the issue of a periodical which is not "substantially the same as" that published elsewhere. Then everybody will know what is involved.
What we are going to find is that an official will make a decision today, and next year a different official or deputy minister charged with that responsibility might make a completely different decision. As my hon. friend for St. Paul's has suggested, it is the lack of knowledge of certainty that I think is so important here. It is not good enough to say that the official makes the decision and if it is not liked appeal can be made to the courts. I do not think that makes sense at all. I think the minister sees what I am driving at, that it is possible to regulate under section 221 if they wish to do so.
