subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to commend the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Roberts) for his intervention and for bringing some very cogent arguments to the debate. After sitting through last night's session and hearing the interventions of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt), the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik), and the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), I thought for a moment that I was in the United States Congress listening to the arguments of the lobbyists for Time and Reader's Digest. It was a most incredible evening.

February 6, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
I have been asked many times why we in the New Democratic Party support this bill. As has been stated, it is an attempt to give some kind of consideration to the Canadian periodical industry and to remove an anomaly whereby in 1965 Time and Reader's Digest, although by all degrees of understanding foreign magazines, were classified under the Imcome Tax Act as Canadian magazines, so that their advertisers could receive the same deductibility provisions as Canadian advertisers in Canadian magazines. The amendment of the hon. member for Ontario which is before us, as amended by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, subverts the whole intent of this legislation.
When we try to decide what is a Canadian magazine, thereby entitling it to the benefit of the provisions of the Income Tax Act so far as advertisers are concerned, four criteria were outlined by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) in testimony before the committee. Two key criteria which I do not think have had enough elaboration in this debate are the licensing and the "substantially different" requirements.
The amendment of the hon. member for Ontario seeks to reduce the amount of material in any given magazine that must be "substantially different" from 80 per cent to 60 per cent. As we have heard in the committee, this would mean continuing an advantage to American magazines whereby they could import the remaining 40 per cent material from the parent magazine, expensive material such as full colour lay-out material, and expensive research material, at a subsidized price. Therefore no Canadian magazine would be able to compete against that kind of advantage.
This has been the problem with the Canadian periodical industry to date. Time and Reader's Digest have been given tax privileges which were reserved for Canadian magazines, and at the same time they had the advantage that no Canadian magazine had of being able to obtain their content from their parent magazine at a subsidized rate. In effect we had editorial dumping in this country.
I am constantly amazed how members of the Conservative party and a few dissident Liberals can make the argument that a Canadian magazine should not have this kind of advantage, and at the same time argue that foreign magazines like Time and Reader's Digest should have that advantage, whereas they do not make the same argument for foreign industry in the manufacturing field. That seems to me to be totally inconsistent.
I think it important that the Minister of National Revenue rise in his place and clarify for the House what is going to happen to the licensing arrangement. There has been an assumption by hon. members and the media that since the Minister of National Revenue's announcement that he had reached an accommodation with Reader's Digest on a continuing arrangement, Reader's Digest would automatically continue to publish in Canada, and that everything had been solved.
I would point out that there are still a number of requirements to which Reader's Digest must conform. I should like the minister to state for the record that Reader's Digest will be required to change its existing licensing arrangement with the parent company in the United States in order to qualify as a truly Canadian magazine. For there exists now a licensing arrangement between Reader's

Digest of Canada and Reader's Digest of the United States whereby Reader's Digest of Canada must, to quote the agreement, not distribute material which the parent disapproves of, or use material from any sources other than those approved by the U.S. parent company
If that licensing provision is allowed to stand, in no way can we conclude that Reader's Digest of Canada is a truly independent Canadian magazine and therefore able to fall within the provisions of section 19 of the Income Tax Act. The minister has assured me in private conversation that Reader's Digest is quite aware that it must change that licensing agreement in order to qualify as a Canadian magazine for income tax purposes. I should like him to state on the record that that is what must happen.
We also learned from the minister that he would allow a continuing arrangement to exist between Reader's Digest Canada and Reader's Digest United States that would not mean that the Reader's Digest edition in Canada would be considered the same as the parent company. The argument put forward by Reader's Digest was that it is the kind of operation that, in order to have access to articles from around the world which should be condensed, it had to have access to the pool of articles collected by Reader's Digest United States.
Therefore the minister made the interpretation saying that as long as Reader's Digest Canada edited, digested, and re-wrote its pool of Reader's Digest articles collected in the United States, that would not be looked at as a continuing arrangement that would violate the 80 per cent different interpretation.
My point is that it seems to me in a roundabout way there still is a degree of editorial control by the parent company which submerges the concept or at least the definition of a truly independent magazine. Let me explain. By virtue of the fact that Reader's Digest United States has pretty well sewn up the market for digest articles, that is to say it has made exclusive arrangements with most of the magazines in North America, if Reader's Digest Canada is to draw on that pool of articles it would seem to me already there has been an editorial decision made by virtue of the fact that the American editors have decided which articles will go into that pool from which the editors of Reader's Digest Canada can draw. So we have, in a sense then, the choice of material to be digested in Canada already being decided upon by American editors, and I think in a roundabout way that puts some constraint on Reader's Digest Canada to be truly independent in choosing the articles it wishes. This is something that must be considered.
Moreover, I fail to see how under that arrangement any new Canadian digest would be able to start up if there is that kind of licensing agreement with the parent company in the United States. I am not speaking of the Canadian Reader's Digest. If we wanted to have a new independent digest, would it be allowed access to this pool of material over which the Reader's Digest in the United States has control? I doubt that that would happen.
There is another point the minister should clarify. One of the requests that the Canadian periodical industry has made, and it is quite valid, relates to the fact that Time and
February 6, 1976

Reader's Digest have had an unfair competitive advantage because they have been able to get their material from their parent companies at a subsidized rate. For example, Reader's Digest can get its material at about 5 per cent of the actual cost of production from its parent company. If Reader's Digest is going to be allowed a continuing arrangement under this new interpretation by the minister we want to have the assurance that Reader's Digest Canada will pay the going rate for these articles which are taken from the pool in the United States, and that the subsidization will not be allowed to continue.
The minister should explain and clarify how the department will go about investigating whether Reader's Digest Canada, under the new interpretation, is paying the going rate that any other magazine would be paying for the right to digest an article from another magazine. If there is any doubt that the Department of Revenue will be able to scrutinize Reader's Digest closely when it purchases articles from this pool of the United States Reader's Digest, then I would have serious reservations about our ability to accept this interpretation.
I am also anxious that the minister clarify the position of Time magazine as it relates to this interpretation of the continuing arrangement, for the minister said in the House, as reported at page 10607 of Hansard:
We are saying that "middle party access" used to obtain third party material will not be regarded as a continuing arrangement.
I asked the minister privately what is to prevent Time magazine from setting up a middle party in the form of a news collection agency, drawing material from correspondents throughout the world, with the material going into a news collection agency just as there is a pool from which Reader's Digest will pull material. From this news collection agency Time United States would draw material and Time Canada would also draw material. If Time is allowed to make that kind of arrangement, similar to Reader's Digest, then again we find a major loophole in the legislation that allows Time to make some kind of a continuing arrangement through setting up a third party or a news collection agency.
The question arises once again, would this material be at a subsidized rate and would Time have sole access to it? I do not think that would be the case because the correspondents may be in the employ of Time and, therefore, under the definition of licensing this would not be permitted. I think we need some clarification of that matter.
Also we need some clarification as to what position it puts MD of Canada in, because it is a similar kind of magazine to Reader's Digest. I would like to know if MD of Canada could set up some parallel licensing or continuing arrangement that would allow it to qualify under the regulations as Reader's Digest apparently has.
Those are the points that should be on the record for clarification, and I hope the Minister of Revenue rises at a later time to clarify them.
We have some difficulty with the fact that so much of this legislation is being done by regulation and at the whim of the Department of National Revenue. It would help matters immensely if this were all spelled out, or if the regulations were in the form of legislation so we do not have continuing variations in interpretations as ministers
Non-Canadian Publications
change, or as time goes on and magazine groups are able to lobby for some kind of change.
In retrospect it is very important that in trying to make accommodations for a magazine to become Canadian we do not subvert the intention of the legislation in the first place. I have no quarrel with Reader's Digest or Time magazine if they conform to the definition of what a Canadian periodical is, as all other Canadian periodicals do. I have no objection to them continuing in this country as long as they continue on the same footing as Canadian magazines.
What I do object to is the kind of legislation we have had for the past decade that has allowed Time and Reader's Digest to be treated as Canadian, although they are not, and therefore has allowed their advertisers income tax advantages reserved only for Canadians. The result has been that Time and Reader's Digest have gained the lion's share of advertising in this country to the detriment of the growth and expansion of the Canadian magazine industry. We heard much testimony to that effect before the committee, and we heard about fluttery flowers last night.
I would remind hon. members that when we look at the figures for the period 1950 to 1974 and when we look at the percentage increase in advertising revenue, we find that for the whole of the Canadian industry in those 24 years their advertising revenue increased by 185 per cent but that the revenue for Reader's Digest, an American subsidiary, increased by 413 per cent while that of Time magazine increased by 819 per cent. Those two magazines have had ten years of operation under tax advantages reserved only for Canadians and have captured over 50 per cent of the advertising revenue in this country. They are immensely rich. They have profited immensely by this legislation.
In the intervening period, however, we have seen Canadian magazines existing on a hand-out basis. We have seen some of them go under, and some almost go under such as Saturday Night. I am not speaking particularly of Maclean's magazine. I would like to see more competition by Canadian magazines against Maclean's. We have heard from many independent journalists that they are on a desperate course and that any advertising revenue which may be diverted their way by virtue of the requirement that Time and Reader's Digest either conform or lose their independence would be governed by their continued growth or collapse.
I think we must keep these points in perspective. This bill has nothing to do with censorship or who will be allowed to publish, but rather who will be assisted in publishing in this country. Therefore I argue very strenuously against the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Ontario and the sub-amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. They subvert the intent of the legislation and should not be supported. In the meantime I would ask the Minister of National Revenue to stand in his place and clarify the implications of the new arrangement with Reader's Digest so that we may debate this issue with some clarity in respect of the new status of that magazine.

February 6, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we must all acknowledge that it is difficult to simplify the legislative process. The amending process, generally speaking, is even more complicated and even more difficult to sort out. The present amendments are no exception. That being so I see no reason to complicate further the matter as is now being done. This is one of the problems that confronts us in the present debate. I shall return to that in due course. The other, the further complication I mentioned, is the government's interpretation of its mandate. I shall now address myself to that.
This bill, and its rocky passage through the House illustrate as clearly as any procedure I can imagine the unusual attitude of the government toward the legislative process, toward the mandate secured at election time, toward the people of Canada, a certain proportion of whom elected members opposite to office, and finally towards the views, wishes, and desires expressed by that population.
Starting at the end of that list, I ask how does the government regard or take into account popular views and concerns? From my particular angle I feel obliged to say that the government feels free to ignore popular concerns, to ride roughshod over them, and to replace them with views which conform more closely to what the government considers the general public should want. That is the way this government governs.
What is its attitude toward the people of Canada? We have seen that already too often and in too many different forms. It regards the people of Canada as a necessary nuisance, necessary to put them in power but thence forward a nuisance, a nuisance with no real mind of its own, no critical faculties and no ability to determine what it wants. Why do I say this? I say this because these are very serious strictures. I believe them to be true. Why? Because of the evidence accumulated before me even on this one bill. It has been built up since the time I have been in this House. However, on this one bill alone there is ample evidence to substantiate my case.
Is there anyone on the government benches who can assure me that he has received one single letter from a reader of Reader's Digest saying, "Kick them out. They're no good. They're anti-Canadian". I would wager that no such letters exist in the files of any parliamentarian. But how many letters are there in my files and in the files of all members of this House, urging that Reader's Digest be left alone to provide the service it performs so well?
What does the government do? The government says in so many words: Now listen, you people out there, you elected us to do a job for you. Go back to your jobs and we will get on with ours which is to provide you with what we know is good for you, not necessarily what you want, but what we, the government, determine that you want. What the government is doing in adopting that attitude is recasting in group terms the definition enunciated by Edmund Burke on the role of elected representatives. Elected representatives by this transposed definition are put in place not to represent the constituents who elected them but rather to do their thinking for them. There are some, I suppose, who may believe this might be possible on a member by member basis, but who other than the government will allow that definition to be transferred to an association of members? This may be the view of members 
of the government but there are not many beyond their number who share it.
My criticism of the government in its approach to legislation in general and this legislation in particular will be developed elsewhere. I leave these comments as they are and turn to another aspect of the measure before us which causes me concern. This is the ability of ministers to interpret laws passed by this parliament. I might say there was an exchange between the minister and the house leader of my party which helped clarify the matter for me. During the lunch period I endeavoured to find where that authority was put forward. I am happy to note that the opposition House leader, with his much wider experience than mine, was able to find it whereas I did not. As he so rightly pointed out, it lies in section 221 (j) of Part XV of the Income Tax Act, which of course is not being touched by the amendments that are being proposed.
We must ask ourselves why we are focusing our attention on Reader's Digest when we learn, through the press and elsewhere, that due to re-definition of a definition the full weight of this legislation will not fall on that publication? Why then should we worry? We have cause to worry, and I suggest Reader's Digest has cause to worry. My particular reason for concern in this area is that if the minister can sharpen a definition, as he has done by pronouncing the 80 per cent substantially different notion under the authority granted to him under 221(j), and then withdraw it, he can just as easily introduce a figure at a later date and suggest an even higher figure. That gap must be closed. I suggest to hon. members that the amendments proposed by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) do just that. They close that gap, and define and narrow the discretion of the minister, as it should be.
The important openings to those two amendments before us, motions Nos. 4 and 5-and I commend both hon. members for having proposed them-read as follows: "notwithstanding the provisions of this Act or Regulations." This is true in both cases. Therefore these amendments override any amendments, regulations, redefinitions, or redefinitions of definitions which might come about by order in council or through the exercise of ministerial discretion.
What do these amendments do? The first one is the more all-embracing. It defines Canadian periodicals in terms of ownership and content. The second one defines ownership and the control and conduct of editorial and publication functions. These are very important definitions. They narrow the scope of interpretation-which unfortunately has been broadened or let loose in so much legislation- and bring within the ambit of parliament the control of the law and the formation and structure of that law. In this House we have complained about the freedom with which governments can play with the law. We see a solution here.
With the statute of 1970-71, the amendments to the Income Tax Act, so much was involved that something slipped through. We found a gap here, and the hon. member for Ontario and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway have closed it and allowed us to give expression-and I come back to the first part of what I had to
February 6, 1976

say-to the views which are passed on to us by way of correspondence and in discussions with our constituents.
I said earlier that surely there is not one hon. member in this House who has not been overwhelmingly deluged with letters, communications, telephone calls, and personal intercessions seeking for the maintenance of the status of at least Reader's Digest. There was less emphasis with regard to Time. Here we have a means of doing so because the formula provided in these two amendments is one with which Reader's Digest at least can comply.
The hon. member for Sault Ste Marie (Mr. Symes), who preceded me, mentioned the matter of two other important publications. Time may come under this category, and if it does that is all well and good. I do not think it can in its present form. However, MD of Canada is certainly a publication which deserves our attention, and I hope it can come within the prescribed limits of ownership, control, and conduct of the editing and publication functions as defined by the second amendment.
Therefore, along with a number of my colleagues I am delighted that these amendments have been proposed, and I can give them my unquestioned support because I feel that this House should do the legislating. Legislation should not be left to order in council, the whim of a minister or ministerial discretion. I have great regard and respect for the minister, but I think it is unfair to impose upon him, along with the many tasks he has confronting him from day to day, the duty of amplifying legislation parliament has passed indifferently or defectively. For that reason I welcome the amendments, and I will give them my support.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to join in this debate to discuss two points. I say to the government or anyone else that the question of 80 per cent content is a myth. It is undefinable and does not exist in the context the government claims in the legislation before us. When we think in terms of percentage, we must realize that we are using a mathematical concept. We are dealing with units or numbers.
It is possible to talk about percentage if we are talking about volume, length, weight, or anything for which we can use a unit of measurement. If we talk about miles, centimetres, kilograms, pounds or anything which is a unit of measurement, we can use the term 80 per cent, but I challenge hon. members opposite, and the minister specifically, to tell us the unit of measurement used with regard to censoring a foreign magazine.
In the committee when this question came up the deputy minister said that the unit of measurement would be one of length. We challenged him by asking if we took a piece of material which was 100 column inches long and reduced it to 20 inches, but it really had the same content material in it, would that be acceptable under the regulation of the government, and he responded, yes. However, the minister interjected and said no, it must be substantially different in content.
The hon. member for Sault Ste Marie (Mr. Symes) said that the government is not into a censorship program. I suggest that it is because if it is saying that the content must be substantially different and it cannot define the unit of measurement, it is a case of the government making
Non-Canadian Publications
the decision and being the judge. The fact of the matter is that this government does not know what the unit of measurement is. It is applying a mathematical concept to a value judgment, which is impossible.
If we are going to talk about a situation in which foreign publications or foreign material comes into this country to be printed and is subjected to a bureaucratic value judgment we must recognize, that as a subjective position, that does not have a unit of measurement. It cannot be measured in percentages-that can only be applied when we speak of weight, length, or volume. We cannot apply percentages to value judgments. Applying mathematical concepts to value judgments implies censorship because it means the government is the judge of what Canadian people will read.
I challenge the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) to give this House some unit of measurement; otherwise the whole concept falls apart. Unless that is forthcoming the government can rule out 100 per cent, or 50 per cent, or whatever it wants. If bureaucracy likes the flavour of some foreign information it can allow it into the country. On the other hand, if bureaucrats do not like something they can censor it 100 per cent. Recognizing there is no unit of measurement is simply a subjective judgment and that means the government is all powerful. It means there is no debate. A group of people in the bureaucracy make a subjective judgment about a piece of writing, but unless they can produce some unwavering criteria to support their judgment then there is no formula.
The other matter I wanted to refer to is the phrase "substantially not the same as previously published material". That there is a fallacy in the legislation has already been admitted in committee. The reference to previously published material in fact means that writers from any other country can publish first in Canada and then in a foreign country. Any material written in another country becomes acceptable if it is first published in Canada, but if it is published in the other country and then comes to Canada it is not acceptable.
All that magazines such as Reader's Digest or MD of Canada have to do is change the order of publication by one month-publish first in Canada and then in the foreign country. "Substantially not the same as previously published material" simply means that you change the order of publishing to escape the regulation. That will not protect the Canadian publishing industry but simply creates a loophole to circumvent the law.
The percentage content is a myth, Madam Speaker. There is no unit of measurement. I hope the Secretary of State will define for us how the 80 per cent figure is arrived at. Unless there is a mathematical basis it becomes a subjective judgment of the government and that essentially means censorship.
Quite frankly I do not see any better evidence of the government's position on the "new society" and a greater degree of government intervention than this legislation which, with the words "80 per cent", grants the government power to restrict the entry of written matter that it does not like or allow material that is advantageous to it. I hope the minister will respond and clear up this matter

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would gladly have yielded the floor to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) whom I thought would perhaps want to give the House some factual information. I have no desire to stand in his way, but he is not in the House at the moment and there are some things I should like to say arising out of the subamendment and the amendment which have been proposed.
It has been emphasized by those supporting the bill that it has a very simple purpose, that is, to eliminate the special status enjoyed substantially by two magazines with large circulations and perhaps by some other specialist types of periodicals.
I want to say quite frankly that I do not favour the maintenance of special status for any periodical-or anybody else as far as that is concerned. That is not my problem with the bill. I have to say in all frankness that it is now apparent that the Minister of National Revenue and the government as a whole are not in fact eliminating special status; they are continuing to maintain a sort of special status for one of the periodicals.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) is shaking his head but I do not think he can convince any fair-minded Canadian that things have not been arranged so that the special circumstances of Reader's Digest will enable it to continue to maintain tax deductible benefits for Canadian advertisers in that publication.
I think it is desirable to eliminate special status. I recognize the problem the Canadian periodicals face. The problem in Canada is not peculiar to publications or periodicals. If I were in a court of law-and were paid to do it-I could make a pretty good argument to the effect that manufacturers and others trying to do business here face the competition of factories which enjoy longer production runs because they serve bigger markets, and so on.
I presume that the minister would argue that publications, television, and so on, are in a special category, in view of their importance to our national and cultural life and that, consequently, their position is different from that of concerns engaged in ordinary lines of business. He would argue, no doubt, that the preservation of their economic health and the encouragement of their development are important for the cultural life of the country. I accept that. But the question I keep asking myself is: does this bill achieve that purpose at all, and achieve it in a satisfactory way? It will not achieve it by making available to other publications advertising which has been monopolized, shall we say, or dominated by Time and Reader's Digest.
I think Reader's Digest is the biggest factor in the field and, under the new interpretation handed down from on high, Reader's Digest will be able to continue publishing in this country. I am not suggesting that Reader's Digest should be pushed out of Canada; I do not mean that. I merely say that the bill will not achieve its purpose, as it now is interpreted. In other words, it will not release all

that advertising for other Canadian publications. That is not my principal objection to what the government is doing.
I am not objecting because the government's bill will be only partially successful under the present interpretation, will only succeed in pushing Time out and releasing only part of the advertising which Time and Reader's Digest have been getting. My real objection, in other words, is not that the government's aim will be only partially achieved; my objection is to the whole way in which the government is proceeding.
I hope the Secretary of State will not take offence if I say to him, as I said earlier in the week, that the government's general procedure is fundamentally dishonest, fundamentally at odds with what I consider as liberal democratic procedure.
Earlier in the week I asked the Secretary of State if he could honestly say that "substantially the same" means the same as "80 per cent the same". I do not know how anyone can argue that such expressions come within the normal use of the English language. How can anyone argue that the interpretation given those words approaches their normal meaning? The interpretation is a complete distortion of the three words "substantially the same". How can one say something must be 20 per cent the same, or 80 per cent different? In other words, the government is changing the statute.
Parliament previously adopted a statute which said that something must be "substantially the same." The government is changing that statute, by executive decree. It is not asking parliament to change the law. The government itself is changing the law. The Secretary of State can argue that that is not the point, that the only thing before the House is the elimination of special status. But what can one say about the meaning the government has given to the phrase "substantially the same?" It has changed the statute by executive decree, a decree which has become part of the res gestae. That action has become an integral, basic, and essential part of the question we are considering. I cannot accept as a member of parliament, and could not accept if I were not in parliament, the idea that members of the government can, under our constitution, arbitrarily change the meaning of a statute passed by parliament.

The House resumed from Monday, November 4, 1974, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fortin:
That, in the opinion of this House, a special committee of inquiry on Crown corporations exercising financial, commercial or industrial activities be established to study the various Acts establishing such Crown corporations, the Crown Corporations Act, sections 76 to 88 of the Financial Administration Act, and all other laws concerning Crown corporations and to recommend to the House the adoption of a law regarding federal public enterprises: the committee should also study the following subjects without restriction (a) the legal rules pertaining to the employees of such corporations (b) their financial structure (c) the way in which they are financed (d) government control over said corporations (e) fiscal regulations (municipal, school, provincial and federal taxes) (/) the status of the administrators (g) the privileges of such corporations resulting from their being "commissioned by Her Majesty" (h) the status of the subsidiaries of these enterprises (i) their purchasing policy (j) the problem of auditing by the auditor General of Canada or by private auditors (k) the appropriateness of State intervention in the economic field in the form of enterprises; and all other matters concerned.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to address the House on the matter raised by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin). The hon. member several times previously has brought forward the subject matter of this motion and has spoken at length and considerable good sense on the subject, the last time being November 4, 1974. That day the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette), on behalf of hon. members on my side,
Crown Corporations
presented a scholarly rendering of the law affecting Crown corporations. He gave a considerable elucidation of the responsibilities they had under the Financial Administration Act. The essence of the motion, as hon. members are aware, is seeking a far greater responsibility for members of parliament to gain information as to the practice, spending procedures and so on, of Crown corporations.
The whole rea of Crown corporations is both interesting and of some concern. Over many years we have found that they have served governments well. They are legal entities set up either to carry out responsibilities for which no other group or aggregate of capital is interested in doing, or there has been a situation of enterprises floundering and requiring government intervention.
The last case of this aspect is with respect to Canadair and de Havilland. The Government of Canada acquired control of those two corporations with the objective of trying to maintain the aircraft industry in Canada, ultimately for the benefit of the country. Hopefully it will be restored to the private sector.
One can look at the history of this country and see cases where Crown corporations have been formed and have grown into great empires, now reaching a value of some $20 billion. Under the regime of Prime Minister R. B. Bennett, Canadian National Railways was put together as well as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the Bank of Canada. All of these institutions were formed under a Tory government, those champions of the private sector. It is sometimes forgotten by Canadians that these bold initiatives were taken for good and sufficient reasons. Since that time, both Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have grown into major, massive corporations which compare in size to their opposite numbers throughout the world as being among the giants, particularly in the case of the railroad.
I suspect that for a good many members, the notion that parliament should have considerable control over the activities of Crown corporations is very appealing. I found it distressing in a committee hearing that when a Crown corporation came up for consideration there was very little time to deal with it, and frequently little information was provided.
The annual reports, like all corporate annual reports, tend to highlight the accomplishments of the year and downgrade that which did not go favourably. There is always a generous tribute to the management, however competent or incompetent it might have been, but that is about all. Members of parliament in rare instances have an opportunity to question the officers of the corporations. They are extremely limited in the opportunity they have to get real information about the affairs of the corporations.
I found it particularly distressing on two occasions that we had officers before us. One instance was that of Canadian Arsenals. The other was the Export Development Bank. In both cases the presidents said it was contrary to law and that they were unable to reveal their annual salary. I personally found that totally unacceptable.
As one who goes home to my constituency regularly and consults my mail every day, I find that my own modest stipend is the subject of constant public interest. When we

I can understand that some of them might be embarrassed to have their large emolument compared with that of a member of parliament. I do not know if that is the primary motivation or not.
Crown corporations cover an extraordinary wide range. We have some 40 of them which represent departmental corporations. They are very much directly responsible to the department and the minister. We have agency corporations which are somewhat less so. We have proprietary corporations such as Canadian National Railways which have great superstructures, the ability to borrow and the ability to finance their own requirements.
Because the hon. member for York East gave such a scholarly rendering of the Financial Administration Act and how it affected these corporations, I suppose hon. members would welcome it if I were to dwell for a few minutes on several of these Crown Corporations, discuss what they do and how they are constituted. What comes to mind is the Seaway International Bridge Corporation Limited. That would be a fascinating subject for discussion.
Also the National Museums of Canada would open a wide range of discussion-for example, the locations of the museums. One's mind runs back to the great full page ads placed by the Victoria Museum when it completed its expensive renovations, advising Canadians as far away as Victoria, B.C. of these changes. They were full page ads to encourage Canadians to visit that museum. I spoke to the minister who confirmed that perhaps this was carrying a good thing a little far. It does perhaps illustrate that these corporations have a way of acting on their own without respect for parliament or even the minister.
When one talks of the problem of Crown corporations not being sufficiently responsible to parliament or to their officers in appearing before us, I think much of this could be said of the whole apparatus of government and the sense of relative futility that we, as members of parliament, feel in trying to analyse and know something about the vast expenditures and what lies behind them. The opportunities for discussing departmental estimates are relatively slight compared to their enormity. I am sure that even the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) must find it difficult to be able, in the hours that he spends in this House, in committees, and in his office, to grasp the whole complexity of government and find himself aware of all these expenditures.

It would be very surprising if we did not see him here. Indeed our children, or grandchildren yet unborn, may find themselves seated in this chamber watching the hon. member participating in these proceedings on a Friday afternoon. I hope that will be the case.
When we talk about Crown corporations being made more accessible to parliament-and I strongly recommend that legislation be enacted in this area-I think it is worth considering what is happening in the private sector. As we all know, there has been considerable debate lately on the subject of free enterprise, public enterprise, a free market system, state socialism and so on. I know all of us are concerned about this vital area of discussion.
It is worth pointing out, I think, that the information which is available to Canadians concerning the affairs of Crown corporations is in a great many respects more comprehensive than that provided to private shareholders by many of the great private corporations. Anyone familiar with the workings of major corporations realizes how little opportunity exists for interrogation of the officers of those corporations or for ascertaining information beyond that which can be read in an annual report. Shareholdings in these corporations are often closely held by blocks capable of exercising control. Before annual meetings take place proxies are sent out, and provision is usually made for half an hour or so to be set aside for questions. The questioning, in these circumstances, is merely a formality. At most, it has only a nuisance value, and as soon as possible everyone repairs to a nice lunch, if it is a good company, and that is "it" for the year.

Madam Speaker, the fact that this motion was introduced 15 or 16 months ago, that is on November 4, 1974, indicates that we have undertaken a long trip. This session could very well be extended to June and perhaps even later, if we take note of progress made in recent days concerning the legislation before us and if we consider other highly controversial bills now being discussed even by the government members.
It is not the first time the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) tackles this matter and brings in an issue that vexes several members. I have before me a letter from a colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski), who make a suggestion to me as a member of the Committee on Procedure and Organization now working on the terms of reference of a sub-committee for the study of our organization of the House of Commons.
He indicated to me that he has a great desire that we should have among all our committees of the House of Commons precisely a committee to study the activities and reports of Crown corporations, and in fact quoted the same arguments put forward by the hon. member for Lotbiniere on November 4. He said that this should be compulsory in order that every Crown corporation be subject to parliamentary scrutiny. Now, he indicated that the last report of Air Canada which has been studied has been the 1970 report, that the answers are always the same, and that when a member asks for information this can be detrimental to the corporation involved.
Now, are all those arguments valid? Also given as examples is the Parliament of the United Kingdom and, among

I am told there are about fifty. Well, they will count them, perhaps there are now sixty. They have just established what I call "Petro-Can". We are asked questions the answers to which hon. members would like to know: What are the salaries of the executives? I do not know what will be the use of knowing that.
Are there any reliable reports published every year by chartered accountants, regardless of whether they come from the Auditor General or the private sector, just as long as they are competent auditors? Those people are every bit as honest and responsible as the Auditor General. To my mind, of the two I would say that the Auditor General is better qualified to say whether the operations of a Crown company are viable or not, and whether they are dishonest.
I do believe my hon. colleague from Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) as well as the hon. member for Lotbiniere wonder if all Crown companies are profitable and justifiable. Why were they created? Some are 40 years old. How were they set up? What were their objectives at the time? Have circumstances changed? At this time, are their activities profitable or do they follow the same old routine without anyone ever questioning their raison d'etre or ever wondering why this Crown corporation should not be disbanded.
I would simply like to point out that this has already been done. I have here a manuscript on a study made by Dr. Allan Blair, associate professor of the Commerce Department at Carleton University, sponsored by the research department of my party. Dr. Blair gives the names of a number of Crown corporations and concludes that they should be ended, that some of their activities could be transferred to other existing corporations or even taken over by the Department of National Defence.
A case in point, Defence Construction Limited. This corporation was established in 1942 or 1943 by then Minister of Munitions C. D. Howe. Why? Because during the war it was necessary to maintain the construction of several army bases in Canada, barracks and what have you. At that time he was not impressed with the efficiency of the Department of Public Works as several scandals later came out in that field. War construction works were to be done as quickly as possible instead of going through the normal procedure, namely the Treasury Board and the Department

of Public Works. Government machinery was much too slow, later on it improved and is now quite efficient.
What is DCL today? It is a Crown corporation which finds itself caught in a little corner of the Department of National Defence. Its directors are civil servants.
There are others, such as the Canadian Arsenals, the Canadian Commercial Corporation and another whose existence hon. members probably do not know: the Canadian National West-Indies Steamship Limited. Why is that? They have two ships.

speechtext: They had two ships.

speechtext:
This corporation exists only to protect certain interests that we must recover on our debts. Others, like St. Clair River Broadcasting Limited and Canadians Arsenals Limited, have special roles to play. I shall read my quotations in English because they are in English and the translation would not be accurate. [English]
With regard to the historical public policy mandate, CAL was the phase-down agent for munitions production at the end of World War II. The mandate "fit" was appropriate at that time. Today it is the custodian and operator of two Crown owned facilities and keeps a skill pool in place. The other day it almost did not; the skill pool nearly left its earthly confines. As for its ongoing public policy rationale, there is none really apparent; phase-out seems appropriate, with skills lodged departmentally. I did say "DCL"; that is, Defence Construction (1951) Limited.
Then we have Eldorado Nuclear Limited and Eldorado Mining and Research. They were expropriated under war emergency powers to control uranium sources exploitation. They were closed down in 1940 when I was working for a subsidiary up on the Mackenzie River and I can assure you that this caused some consternation among the employees. However, they were resurrected in 1942. What should happen to these two companies? A thorough review and study are recommended. This was first recommended in 1961 and I think should be carried out. I could go down all the way through this list.

I shall come back to the purpose of the committee because I believe that if the motion of the hon. member were adopted, we would launch a perpetual and comprehensive investigation which would never come to any conclusions. We may wonder why, especially if the terms of reference cover only one session of Parliament. I would agree entirely with the hon. member that this committee, whether it be a joint committee or a committee of the House only, should be a small committee, including a maximum of six or eight members well versed on the subject who could examine the philosophy and the purpose of Crown corporations. This commission should be asked to make recommendations like those made by Dr. Blair.
I cannot say that I would not accept this, because I did not study the report carefully, but several corporations should be eliminated, others should be modified and others should be clarified because many of them were established 30 or 40 years ago.

The Crown corporation has a very viable and very valid role but simply because the child was born many years ago I would not say it necessarily follows that it must continue to operate. If that is the case, I can speak of another objective, in addition to those that were put forward by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin), and others who spoke on this subject. It is difficult to remember, and I would be quite prepared to recommend strongly to the government that if this motion cannot even be passed this could be taken into consideration and amended to examine the principles of Crown corporations.
In our day-to-day activities if we want to consider something and pass a judgment we must make sure we know what we are talking about. Otherwise, there is no point in entering the ring. You do not send a carpenter to examine the inside of a stomach, you ask the doctor, an expert. And to say here that a group of members could examine accurately and rightly the administration, say of Air Canada, what do they know about it? Quite simply, there would have to be a whole body of examiners and our committee would have to form a jury rather than simply saying we are going to conduct the examination and we as members are going to ask the questions. Somehow we would come out of it. We would push a little button or ask a question to an official or an executive of, say Air Canada or the CNR, and a fountain would immediately spout all the information required.
I prefer that we start by limiting our objective, then the little commission of inquiry of this House would hire competent staff and take a company or two and examine them. Then the commission could pass a judgment, make recommendations to the government and continue to amend or stiffle that corporation.
Those are my views on this point and I thank hon. members as well as you, Madam Speaker, for the attention you gave me.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased and honoured to comment on this motion moved by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) recommending the establishment of a special committee of inquiry on Crown corporations engaged in financial, commercial, or industrial activities.
With all due respect to the hon. member, one of the things that struck me a year and a half ago when I became aware of these august halls for the first time was the great complexity, not only of Crown corporations, but of the government as a whole. At that time the question came to my mind how one person who is responsible for representing an area could possess the ability to understand all of these complex things and at the same time deal efficiently with the many matters that arise in his riding. How does an hon. member grasp, within a reasonable period of time,
Crown Corporations
the many complexities with which we are faced on a day-to-day basis here?
I suppose many of us here are a bit lost in respect of this vast area of enterprise in which the government is involved. I suppose it comes down to the question of what is the role of an hon. member in this House, and to what activities should he direct his energies. It is for that reason I am pleased to speak on this motion.
We sometimes forget that we were not sent here as accountants to go through the books of various corporations. I was under the impression we were sent here to act as legislators. We have accountants, lawyers, and many other people employed in government service. We must assume first of all that they are basically honest and fairly intelligent, and that the information they provide members is accurate.
We must operate with the information that is available to us and make decisions for the betterment of the country. I for one would still be lost having gone through the financial statements of some of our many Crown corporations. They are part of the vast galaxy of shoot-offs from our government. For example, there is the centennial commission. I have no idea what that is. Since we have had our 100 years celebration perhaps this no longer is in effect. It may be that someone has not noticed that it is still in existence. This is an example of the vastness of this area.
In deference to my compatriot across the floor, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who has been in this House for many years, he might tell me whether in his many years' experience he has discovered how Crown corporations operate and whether he has a greater knowledge about them now than he had previously. If I am not mistaken there are approximately 250 people whose job is to act as auditors for the government. They are employed by the Department of the Auditor General. I would not wish that job on anyone. It must be a tremendous undertaking.
I believe the previous Auditor General required additions to his staff. I hope there is now sufficient staff in the Department of the Auditor General because, from a look at the number of corporations as well as the departments, it would seem that this must be an enormous task.
I wonder whether any member of this House or any committee of this House should try to take away the power or the right of review by the Auditor General's department. I wonder even if we did decide that was in the interest of Canada and the House, whether we or members of the committee, with our backgrounds which are unrelated to accountancy, actually would make any contribution to this House or the government. It might be that we should examine our priorities. As much as I may be in sympathy with the motion of the hon. member I wonder what, in practical terms, it would accomplish. I wonder how deeply we would be able to go into the situation and how much time would be required. Also I wonder whether we could afford such an in-depth study.
If such a study were to be meaningful it could not be conducted over night or once, say, every five or ten years. It would have to be an on-going process. The expertise

required might be outside our sphere. This is a debatable subject.
In the past perhaps a band-aid approach has been taken to this. Situations have arisen which caused the government and the House to take a certain course of action. Special committees of the House have been established for the purpose of examining the situation in respect of a Crown corporation or something else. Although this may be open to debate, it would seem to me that this is a reasonable way to do it.
If a situation should develop among one of the corporations which we feel is wrong, or in respect of which we feel there is some question concerning the competence of the people involved, perhaps a special committee to study that situation is the answer. I suppose a good example is the special committee that was set up to study the question of egg marketing. That was a very complex issue. The committee spent several months studying that situation. At the end I felt that there was much more we could have done had we had more time, but I think the House and the committees realize that time is one of our most precious commodities and one of the things of which we do not have very much.
I do not know whether the hon. member who brought in this motion has considered this aspect of having a special committee study certain corporations, or whether he feels that this would not be an ongoing process. However, as one member of parliament I sincerely believe that we must give offices such as that of the Auditor General, once it has been given the job of acting as a watchdog, an opportunity to carry out that function without appointing another watchdog to watch the watchdog.
The reports of the Auditor General are available to us. I have had an opportunity to look at them. It is a difficult task to study these reports. For a lay person who has perhaps no special skill or training in reading columns of figures it is neither the most productive nor easy reading. I believe the hon. member brought up a very important point. As legislators I do not think individually or even as a committee we have the time to go through the reams and reams of statistics in respect of every Crown corporation.
I agree with the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Abbott) that we have the right to know what these people who are running Crown corporations are costing the taxpayers of Canada. It is public money that is being spent and therefore, in my opinion, it should be accounted for.
In the province of British Columbia the salaries of doctors who are paid through the medicare program have been made public because they are paid from money out of the public purse. There was much debate in respect of whether or not the salaries of the doctors should be made available. However, it was decided that since this was public money it should be accounted for.
I have always felt that since we ourselves are under scrutiny, and since we are accountable to the people for the management of the public purse, the money paid to people employed through the Government of Canada should be accounted for and the figures made available. I do not suggest this in a critical way but rather so that it may be ascertained whether the salaries are fair. I am saying this not only from the negative point of view but from the

point of view of making sure that these people are dealt with fairly and equitably and so that we will know whether these expenditures are too high or too low. I think we have the right to know this since we provide the money.
I also strongly believe that the House of Commons should have a status that is higher than that of a court of inquiry. There may be occasions when we might like to delve into that problem. However, I do not see this matter as being a preoccupation of the standing committees. We have many other facilities for studying the problems in various areas of our government service. We should tackle one area alone.
Perhaps as a final comment I might say that this whole question of being able to have the time to go into an area in which we perhaps have specialized would be made much easier if some of the staff we have in our research centres were under our own control rather than being part of a central research staff where we have basically no control over the work done, or the type of person employed. I think at some point the House should consider having an individual member given the right to have his own staff so that he would have someone to work in his office whom he could trust, and whose abilities he would know, so that the member would know the quality of the work being done and so that there would be a much more positive and closer relationship than exists at the present time.
This is slightly off the point made by the hon. member attacking the question of information being made available, but I think all of us have certain interests which could be better researched if we had that sort of staff rather than using the staff under the present system. I realize that this does not include ministers. I am talking about ordinary backbenchers in this House who could make a more positive contribution if they were provided with better research facilities. The information is there if someone has the time to research it, but hon. members know that our time is very limited. Our time is devoted to committee work, the House and so forth, and surely we can use people who have expertise in certain areas to do some of that work for us.
Going back to my original point, that the Auditor General has a branch which is already set up, I do not think we have to go further and set up a watchdog committee. Someone might be interested in Air Canada or, in the case of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), a steamship company-I did not realize we had one in the West Indies, but apparently we have two flag carriers in that area-but all hon. members might not be interested in that. That is why I feel a committee is not the answer. However, if one or two hon. members were interested in a particular subject, they could do the research themselves and that would not take up the time of a committee. We have enough problems.
In the External Affairs Committee we set up a subcommittee to deal with international development. We have problems maintaining interest, although it started off with a great burst of confidence. After CIDA, and where the money was going, had been discussed for several weeks we found that the interest of the committee waned to some extent.
February 6, 1976

I feel we would have the same situation in the committee the hon. member suggests because although one interesting thing might come up, this would not occupy the attention of 16, 20 or 30 people on a month by month basis if it were a permanent committee. For that reason I ask the House to consider this proposal very seriously, to consider whether we already have instruments set up to look into these subjects and whether we would be duplicating efforts. Although I would like to see some way of developing a better research centre for our own members, I cannot agree with the proposal of a permanent committee.
